summary: The most probable root cause is upstream LLM provider rate limiting of llm-gateway starting at about 13:55Z. 429s, retries with backoff and fallback model use rising to 40% slowed and failed llm-gateway, which is the orchestrator's highest-weight synchronous dependency. Orchestrator latency and error rate stepped up in the same minute and then plateaued at a high level. The inbound-msgs backlog from 14:00 is most likely a downstream effect of slow consumers, not a separate cause. The cause of the 429s themselves (provider quota change or traffic growth) is not established. The early msg-delivery receipt-delay warnings (from 13:37Z) are unexplained and may be a separate minor issue.

hypotheses.statement: The upstream LLM provider began rate limiting llm-gateway at about 13:55Z (429s, retries with backoff, fallback model use rising to 40%), which slows and fails the orchestrator's highest-weight synchronous call and so produces slow or timed-out assistant replies.
hypotheses.label: high

supporting.text: Provider 429s begin at 13:55:20Z, with retries and backoff, and fallback model use is first logged at 13:55:34Z and rises to 0.4 by 13:58.
llm-gateway err_rate and latency_ms first deviate from baseline at 13:55, and llm-gateway error rate peaked at 0.258 with latency up to several seconds.
Orchestrator err_rate rose from 0.004 to 0.041 at 13:55 and its latency climbed to about 2.8 s by 13:58 before plateauing, matching the llm-gateway onset.

Orchestrator calls llm-gateway synchronously with the highest weight (0.7), so a degraded gateway plausibly dominates reply latency. It is likely that this is the main driver, though the link is inferred from timing and call weights.

No deploy, config, migration or flag change touched llm-gateway, and the only deploys in the period were copy-only changes to order-router, auth-kyc and aa-sync, so internal changes are an unlikely trigger.

contradicting.text: One-minute samples cannot order the orchestrator rise relative to the first 429 at 13:55:20, so causation (versus coincidence or reverse order) is not shown by timing alone.
No recorded internal change explains the 429 onset. If the provider quota changed or traffic grew, that is outside the tracked data and unverified, so the underlying trigger remains unknown.
A provider latency warning at 13:35:10Z predates the 429s, so provider degradation may have started earlier than the rate limiting.

hypotheses.statement: The inbound-msgs backlog is a secondary effect: the fixed 4 orchestrator consumers drain slowly because each message now waits on the degraded llm-gateway path, so the queue grows from about 14:00 and delays replies and downstream outbound notifications. A separate consumer capacity or consumer fault is the alternative reading.
hypotheses.label: low

supporting.text: The inbound-msgs backlog appears from 14:00:06Z (202 ready) and reaches 2642 by 14:59 with the consumer count fixed at 4. Orchestrator consumes inbound-msgs, so a backlog would delay replies.

It is likely that consumers are not keeping up (growth of about 41 messages per minute), which is an inference from log lines and not a measured consume rate. Orchestrator publishes to outbound-msgs, linking the backlog to notification delays.

contradicting.text: Orchestrator latency and errors rose at 13:55, before the 14:00 backlog onset, so the backlog cannot be the initiating cause of the slowdown.
RabbitMQ latency and error metrics stayed flat, and wa-webhook shows no degradation, so there is no sign of a broker fault or an inbound surge.

hypotheses.statement: A redis-cache hot-context stampede, as in INC-0440, is forcing expensive recomputation that slows the orchestrator and portfolio-svc paths and delays notifications.
hypotheses.label: low

supporting.text: A past incident (INC-0440) had identical symptoms and was caused by a Redis cache stampede. This is a precedent only and is not evidence about this incident.

contradicting.text: Redis shows no evictions and only a small hit-ratio dip to 0.9 at the end of the window, whose onset time is unknown.
Postgres is healthy (no pool queuing, stable latency), and no change records touch Redis or the reply path.
The 429 errors and fallback use in llm-gateway are not explained by a cache stampede.

hypotheses.statement: The late notifications have a separate cause in the notification path (msg-delivery receipt processing or outbound-msgs consumption). Receipt-delay warnings began at 13:37Z, before the 429s and the reply slowdown, so they are not purely downstream of the orchestrator.
hypotheses.label: low

supporting.text: msg-delivery logged delayed-receipt warnings starting at 13:37:17Z, before the 429s and the reply slowdown. There were 10 in total, spread from 13:37 to 14:58 and not clustered at 14:00.
It is possible that the notification path has its own cause, but this is an untested hypothesis.

contradicting.text: msg-delivery latency and error metrics stayed flat and it had no restarts, which does not match the warnings. The two sources disagree and cannot be reconciled.
RabbitMQ shows no WARN lines mentioning outbound-msgs, though this does not prove outbound-msgs is healthy.

assumptions.text: The llm-gateway provider rate limiting (429s) from about 13:55Z is the likely driver of orchestrator latency and errors, since orchestrator's slowdown follows llm-gateway's. This is not confirmed by timing data for orchestrator.

Average growth of inbound-msgs depth is about 41 messages per minute over the hour (roughly (2642-202)/59 min), which suggests consumers are not keeping up with publishes. This is an inference from the log lines, not a measured consume rate.

The reply slowdown most likely originates in a synchronous dependency of the orchestrator (most likely llm-gateway, the highest-weight call) rather than in the queues. This is inferred from call weights and the lack of config or flag changes, not observed.

Orchestrator and llm-gateway degraded in the same minute (13:55Z), and the 429 onset at 13:55:20Z falls in that minute too (E-005). This is consistent with E-010 but does not establish that llm-gateway caused the orchestrator slowdown, because 1-minute samples cannot order events within a minute.

Because the first msg-delivery warning (13:37Z) precedes the 14:00 onset and the 13:55Z 429s, notification delay may have its own cause and not be solely a consequence of the orchestrator slowdown. This is a hypothesis to test, not a confirmed finding.
No recorded change explains a provider quota or rate-limit change on llm-gateway. The 13:55Z 429s may come from provider-side limits or from traffic growth, which is not verified.

Orchestrator degradation starts at or about the same time as llm-gateway 429 onset (13:55), and the 429s are the likely trigger. Minute buckets cannot confirm whether the latency rise came before or after the first 429 at 13:55:20. This weakly supports the earlier hypothesis E-010, and it does not show that the backlog caused the slowdown.

No recorded internal change explains the 429 onset at 13:55:20Z (E-005). The provider-side quota or rate-limit change, if any, is most likely outside this change-tracking system (for example, in the provider console or a contract change), so the 429s are more likely caused by external traffic or quota limits than by an internal deploy.

unresolved: Why the provider began returning 429s: provider quota or rate-limit change, or traffic growth. Request volume for llm-gateway was not pulled and the provider's limits are not visible.
The ordering of the orchestrator rise and the first 429 within the 13:55 minute is unresolved, as is possible clock skew.

actions.text: Check the LLM provider console for quota or rate-limit settings and usage on llm-gateway's account. If the quota was lowered or reached, raise it or request a higher limit.
actions.rationale: 429s began at 13:55:20Z with no internal change, so the provider-side limit is the most likely source and is not visible to the tracked data.

actions.text: Reduce load on the provider path while limits persist: tune llm-gateway retry and backoff, and review how fallback model routing is behaving (currently at 40%).
actions.rationale: Retries with backoff and heavy fallback use are slowing the orchestrator's highest-weight synchronous call.

actions.text: Monitor inbound-msgs depth and, if it continues to grow once the gateway recovers, consider temporarily adding orchestrator consumers to drain the backlog.
actions.rationale: The backlog reached 2642 messages with a fixed 4 consumers and delays replies and downstream notifications.

actions.text: Pull llm-gateway request rate and token volume (rps, tokens_per_min) before 13:55Z, and compare with wa-webhook inbound volume, to find out whether traffic growth triggered the 429s.
actions.rationale: A traffic increase as the trigger is neither confirmed nor excluded.

actions.text: Investigate the msg-delivery receipt-delay warnings separately: check outbound-msgs queue depth, consumer count and msg-delivery INFO logs.
actions.rationale: The warnings began at 13:37Z, before the 429s, and the flat metrics contradict them, so the notification path may have its own cause.

actions.text: Add alerting on llm-gateway 429 count and fallback_pct, and on inbound-msgs depth, and consider a 429_count metric (it does not exist today).
actions.rationale: The 429 timeline came only from log lines, and the backlog was only visible through WARN logs.

actions.text: Reconcile the conflicting metric summaries for orchestrator and llm-gateway latency and obtain sub-minute data to order the first 429 against the orchestrator rise.
actions.rationale: Two queries disagree on peak and last values, and one-minute buckets cannot establish the ordering.
